tagline: Three desert summits on a highway renamed for UFO reports.
intro: Nevada’s SR 375 crosses mostly unoccupied desert along the northern edges of the Nellis Air Force Range, climbing over three summits between Warm Springs and Crystal Springs. It remains lightly traveled. The state named it the Extraterrestrial Highway in 1996 after travelers reported UFOs near Area 51; the Nevada Commission on Tourism sought the name to attract visitors.

The road’s earlier changes came from military restrictions. An unimproved route existed by 1932 as SR 25A, becoming part of SR 25 the next year. By 1957 its western end had shifted to Warm Springs to avoid the testing range, taking the road north of the Reveille Range instead of across the Kawich Range. Paving was complete the following year. Nevada’s 1976 highway renumbering made this western section SR 375, a number first printed on the official state highway map in 1978.

From US 6 at Warm Springs, follow the base of the Reveille Range into Railroad Valley, then climb Queen City Summit, the road’s highest point at 5,935 feet. Descend into Sand Spring Valley and Rachel, then cross Coyote Summit toward Tikaboo Valley and Mail Box Road. Hancock Summit is the last crossing before the route ends at SR 318 in Crystal Springs.

moments.title: Rachel
moments.text: Rachel’s time capsule came from the producers of Independence Day in 1996 and is intended to be opened in 2050. That April, film stars joined state officials in town for the highway’s public dedication. The town began in 1973, founded by alfalfa farmer D.C. Day, and was first called Tempiute Village, then Sand Springs. In 1978 it took the name of Rachel Jones, the first baby born in the valley. When Rachel Jones died in 1980, residents created a cemetery and memorial park in her memory. The capsule is installed near the Little A’Le’Inn.

moments.title: Mail Box Road
moments.text: The Black Mailbox kept its name even after its color changed. It marked Mail Box Road, a dirt route from SR 375 toward restricted land surrounding Area 51. People searching through the original mailbox prompted its replacement with a more secure white one. The spot became a gathering place for UFO seekers, but owner Steve Medlin removed the mailbox because of continued vandalism.

moments.title: Crystal Springs
moments.text: A junction and a few trees mark Crystal Springs at the southeastern end of SR 375. The ghost town stands where SR 375 meets SR 318, northwest of US 93. Silver ore discovered here in 1865 led to its becoming Lincoln County’s first seat, from 1866 to 1867, before Hiko replaced it. Nearby springs and marshes along the White River supply irrigation to ranches and farms. Nevada Historical Marker 205 identifies the ghost town. The nearby springs also supplied water to people traveling the Mormon Trail through this part of Nevada.
